OpenAI Launches Next-Generation Reasoning Model That Outperforms Human Experts

By Alex Rivera | May 12, 2026 | 3 min read

OpenAI has unveiled its latest reasoning model, codenamed Orion, which the company claims surpasses human expert performance on a broad range of scientific and engineering benchmarks. The announcement marks a significant milestone in the race toward artificial general intelligence and is likely to intensify competition among AI labs worldwide.

According to OpenAI's internal evaluations, Orion scores in the 97th percentile on standardised medical licensing exams, achieves near-perfect results on graduate-level mathematics problems, and can autonomously complete multi-step software engineering tasks that previously required teams of experienced developers working over several days.

The model's architecture introduces a novel "chain-of-verification" mechanism that allows it to cross-check its own reasoning before producing a final answer. This self-auditing capability dramatically reduces the rate of confident but incorrect outputs, a long-standing weakness in large language models sometimes called hallucination.

Sam Altman, OpenAI's CEO, described Orion as "the most capable AI system we have ever built" and suggested that the company expects it to play a central role in accelerating scientific discovery. "We are already seeing it make novel contributions in protein-folding research and drug candidate screening," Altman said during a live-streamed press event.

Not everyone is enthusiastic. A coalition of AI safety researchers published an open letter urging caution, arguing that systems capable of outperforming human experts in open-ended domains require substantially more interpretability research before widespread deployment. The letter has gathered over two thousand signatures from academics and industry practitioners since it appeared online this morning.
